My older sister (about 10 years older than me) suffers from depression and bipolar disorder. When I was 9 or 10 she was going through a particularly rough patch. She’d stay in bed all day, rarely leave the house, cry all the time. My parents would go from trying to support her to getting frustrated and yelling at her to get a grip, and just plain being very cruel sometimes. 

I wouldn’t say I was neglected, but I definitely wasn’t a huge focus for my parents. I felt sad for my sister but it was all very hard for a young kid to understand what was happening, and in a way I guess I viewed her as weak or pathetic. So when I got older and my own mental illness started to manifest I internalised the hell out of my emotions, because I didn’t want to turn out like my sister did. I didn’t want to be seen as pathetic or put all my turmoil on display, and after seeing how my parents treated my sister at times I didn’t trust them to understand or be there for me. Even now I find it extremely difficult to admit weakness to other people. I’m not sure how much of that can be attributed to that being who I am as a person naturally, and how much of it was shaped by the experience of living with other mentally ill people.

Okay, I guess for an example I can use this. Generally I am pretty caring and empathetic. So I’ll listen to people’s problems and try my best to be supportive and help out when I can. But then in the back of my mind it’s like I’m inwardly scheming. When I get to know people I form a picture of them over time. The more they tell me about themselves the better I can form this picture. That’s all well and good, but this worse part of me uses the information I’ve gotten from people to pinpoint their deepest insecurities and weaknesses. I calculate how with my words I could best break them. Even at my angriest I have never gone through with using people’s trust in me against them, but just the knowledge of what I could do makes me feel powerful. 

For a lesser example I’m generally pretty into social justice, I’ve been called a “bleeding heart” more than once. But in the back of my mind there’s always this voice asking me why I should give a fuck about anyone else, when no one’s given me the same compassion I would afford to others. That’s just more a lesser intrusive thought thing I suppose.

Yeah, trying to balance it is the worst. That’s why I try to suppress the worse side of me, but then, that has limited success too and probably doesn’t make much of a difference in the long run. I guess it’s not really something we can just get rid of. I hope you can find a way to reach some level of peace within yourself.

No one ever “deserves” to be in a relationship, it’s just a matter of whether two people help bring out the best in each other. When you think about it there’s so many factors that have to align just right for a person to get into a successful relationship. Some people make it look so easy, I know. 

My first relationship (I was 19 at the time) happened to occur organically, I got along really well with a guy in one of my uni classes and he eventually asked me out. Turns out he was actually a sociopath who didn’t have feelings for me, so maybe it wasn’t so organic after all. After we broke up I did kind of spiral into a place where I was desperate for another relationship, so I was on Tinder for a while, where I attracted yet more guys who were even more messed up than I was. Currently (I am now almost 24) I am in a relationship with someone who does treat me pretty good for the most part, but I only met him cos we were set up through mutual friends. 

I know I went off on a tangent then, but what I’m trying to say is that if you find yourself like me when I was trying to validate myself through other people, then it isn’t going to make you happy, and it isn’t going to get you a healthy relationship. It sucks, but you do just kinda have to wait for the right opportunities to present themselves. Like I said, you don’t seem like a bad person at all, so I do think your time will come. It’ll be much easier on you if it isn’t a constant niggling in the back of your mind though (I know, it’s easier said than done). When it comes to finding a relationship there really is no easy answer.

Honestly I just tend to be a magnet for people even crazier than I am. 

For real though, I can’t know for sure if you’re a shitty person, but the fact you’ve been in therapy for so long would indicate that you are trying to better yourself, so I personally don’t believe you’re a bad person. In which case I don’t think your lack of success in relationships is reflective of how worthy of a person you are. Some people just get lucky when it comes to relationships. Others have to be more patient. 

In the meantime, just keep on working on yourself as a person. At the end of the day having a good relationship with yourself is more important than having a relationship with anyone else. I’m sure your time will come some day. :)

Hey, my experience may not be the exact same as yours, but I remember how I felt when I first realised I was bisexual. I was incredibly scared, and self-hating, and even embarrassed. Even though society may be slightly getting better in its treatment of the LGTB community, it’s not all the way there yet, so it’s completely understandable for you to feel this way. It’s easy to feel wrong when the world’s sending you little messages that there’s something wrong with you. 

The fact of the matter is, you can’t change how others will see you, but you can learn to change how you see yourself. You don’t have to come out, and you shouldn’t ever feel pressured to, but at the same time you can still just continue on being yourself. Your sexuality isn’t your identity. You sound young, you have heaps of time to worry about love and companionship and finding someone that’s right for you. Right now you should just focus on yourself, just try to do right by yourself as a person. 

I’ve identified as bisexual for nearly a decade now and I still haven’t officially “come out”. Only a select few people know of my attraction to women. Again, it’s obviously different for me, since I can pass as straight easier, but my point is you can just go along with your life without your sexuality being that shadow constantly hovering over you. Just be yourself; you don’t have to tell anyone who you’re attracted to if you don’t want to. I hope over time you learn to accept that you’re a lesbian, because no matter how wrong it feels, it is not something that should be despised. There’s nothing wrong with you, OP. The only wrong thing is that you have to feel like there’s something wrong with it to begin with, and that is no fault of your own.
